creator: Sabine Hossenfelder
title: Quantum Computing Failure Now Obvious
full_text:
Quantum computing has been one of the
most, if not the most, anticipated new
technology on the horizon.
But things haven't been going as many in
the industry thought they would.
Nevertheless, they're more optimistic
today than ever. What explains this
weird mismatch? Today, [snorts] I have
an explanation for this and also
clarification on my opinion about
quantum computing. Just last week, we
saw another claim of quantum advantage,
this time from IBM and researchers at
the University of Chicago. Quantum
advantage means that a quantum computer
did a calculation that would have taken
unfeasibly long on a conventional
computer. It doesn't necessarily mean
that the calculation had any particular
use. Indeed, in this new example, as
well as in many previous ones, the
calculation is to produce a random
distribution of values. It's got no
known use. There have been other
previous claims that quantum advantage
has been achieved, but as the
philosopher Aram Harrow just nicely
summarized in a new paper, within 18
months of any of these demonstrations,
they've all been reproduced on a
conventional computer or at least been
shown to be reproducible. The one
exception he names was one of those
random sampling cases. Harrow is blunt
with his judgement. He writes, "A
demonstration that a hardware can run a
circuit and that the circuit produces an
observable matching a known answer is a
demonstration of competent diagnostic
engineering. The press cycle of the past
several years has conflated such results
with computational advantage, and the
conflation has been productive of
funding without being productive of the
matter fact under investigation." What
Harrow is referring to is that 5 years
ago, many thought that quantum computers
would already have a commercial use even
when they're small and noisy. This has
been referred to as noisy intermediate
scale quantum computing NISQ for short.
For example, in 2017,
researchers from Google claimed that we
contend that short-term returns are
possible with the small devices that
will emerge within the next 5 years.
Didn't happen. In 2018, researchers from
IBM said that in the near term NISQ
computers have the best potential to
deliver business advantage. One of them
also said that IBM sees the next few
years as the dawn of the commercial
quantum era. Didn't happen. The quantum
computing firm IonQ said in its 2021
annual report, "During the NISQ
computing era, we expect quantum machine
learning to be the first solution to
transition into broadly available
applications." Didn't happen. Enrique
Solana, one of the founders of the
German startup Keepler Quantum, said
that we work to reach a NISQ advantage
for use cases within 18 to 36 months.
That was on August 11th, 2023, almost
exactly 36 months ago. Didn't happen.
These claims from researchers then
spilled over into marketing analysis.
The Boston Consulting Group, for
example, predicted in 2019 that we
anticipate value for end users in these
sectors to reach a relatively modest 2
to 5 billion by 2024. The value to end
users turned out to be even more modest,
namely nil. Today, the only profitable
quantum application has been forecasting
profitable quantum applications. In my
mind, the idea that NISQ computers would
have any commercial uses was obviously
and I mean 11 out of 10 on the
meter. If you need evidence of
this other than my word, I'll pretend to
be deeply insulted but refer you to John
Preskill, one of the world's experts on
quantum computing, who for all I know
termed the phrase NISQ and who famously
did not claim these devices would have
any commercial use. Yes, sometimes the
relevant bit is what they don't say. So,
what I think happened is that academia
leaked into industry and
consulting firms and no one was there to
clean up the mess. No one except
possibly Scott Aaronson, who's been
saying all along that quantum computers
are super interesting from a research
perspective, but commercial advantage,
well, let's not talk about it. Let me be
clear, I'm not saying that quantum
computers will never have a commercial
use. I just think it'll take a long time
to get there, certainly not in this
decade and the uses will be extremely
niche and limited, not a billion-dollar
market. I've noticed that people call me
pessimistic when it comes to quantum
computers. I think I'm not. It's just
that even my most optimistic self thinks
it's idiotic that quantum computers will
bring a new industrial revolution as
some headlines put it. At least
confidence has reached fault tolerance.
I also want to remind you that Demis
Hassabis, who I've put down as one of
the most intelligent people on the
planet, has argued that whatever quantum
processes happen in nature will likely
have so many regularities you can model
them with AI on a conventional computer.
I think scientists aren't taking him
seriously enough. If my day had any more
hours, I'd try to formalize this into a
formal conjecture, but the way things
are going, AI will probably beat me to
it. The last time I wrote code, it was
Fortran.
This is why I decided I need to urgently
upgrade my coding skills. If you're in a
similar situation, I have a
recommendation for you. boot.dev, who've
been sponsoring this video. boot.dev is
focused on backend development, so
Python, SQL, Go, the kind of stuff that
actually runs the world behind the
scenes. And you don't just watch
lessons, you build real projects. You
write code directly in the browser, you
solve challenges, and you level up like
it's a slightly nerdy role-playing game.
They also have what they call the
training grounds, that's basically
infinite practice problem. I've been
meaning for a while to set up a website
for all my content, but I want to know
what's going on with the data and what
vulnerabilities to watch out for, and
boot.dev has been really eye-opening.
You can create an account for free, read
and watch all the content, and try a
demo of the interactive features. If you
decide to go for the full experience,
use my code Sabina to get 25% off your
first year. So, go and check this out.
Thanks for watching. See you tomorrow.

notes.note: The exception cited is not a random-sampling case. Amit Hagar's stated exception is Google's Quantum Echoes/OTOC experiment, designed to differ from random circuit sampling by producing verifiable expectation values, not unverifiable random bitstrings.
notes.claim: The one exception Aram Harrow named to quantum advantage claims being reproduced on conventional computers was one of the random sampling cases.
notes.context_quote: The one exception he names was one of those random sampling cases.
notes.context_paragraph: within 18 months of any of these demonstrations, they've all been reproduced on a conventional computer or at least been shown to be reproducible. The one exception he names was one of those random sampling cases.

sources.quote: With a single clear exception, every NISQ-era flagship demonstration of 'quantum advantage' has... been classically reproduced
sources.explanation: Confirms the existence of exactly one exception in Hagar's paper.

sources.quote: As of this past year, however, we have some strong candidates for verifiable quantum advantage. One is the Google OTOC experiment, as even Hagar himself acknowledges (that’s his “single clear exception”).
sources.explanation: Explicitly identifies that Hagar's 'single clear exception' is the Google OTOC experiment, not a random sampling case.

sources.quote: The heart of the algorithm is measuring the expectation value of a quantum observable, called the out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC).
sources.explanation: Confirms the exception is based on expectation values.

sources.quote: However, this random circuit sampling approach has limited practical utility since the same bitstring never appears twice in a large quantum system, restricting its ability to reveal useful information.
sources.explanation: Distinguishes the OTOC experiment from the previous 'random circuit sampling' approach.

sources.quote: Unlike bitstrings, quantum expectation values, e.g., current, velocity, magnetization and density, are verifiable computational outcomes
sources.explanation: Supports the claim that the experiment produces verifiable values rather than random bitstrings.

notes.opus_reason: "The one exception he names was one of those random sampling cases" is Sabine's own summary of the paper, not something she is quoting from someone else, and it is wrong. I checked Hagar's paper directly: section 4 says "The October 2025 Quantum Echoes experiment is the one demonstration of the period that stands neither reproduced nor closed by theorem, and it is also the one that conforms least to the flagship template", and the same section explicitly puts the December 2024 Willow random-circuit-sampling claim on the other side, as a result closed within ten months by a simulability theorem. Scott Aaronson's post of 18 July 2026 says the same thing ("One is the Google OTOC experiment, as even Hagar himself acknowledges (that's his 'single clear exception')"), so both sources the note leans on check out. The correction matters to her argument, because her point one minute earlier is that these demonstrations produce random distributions with no known use, and the single surviving one is in fact the experiment built to return a verifiable expectation value instead of random bitstrings. The one thing that could draw pushback is that Hagar calls this exception contested and spends a paragraph doubting the 65-qubit accuracy claim, so she may answer that Quantum Echoes still runs on random circuits; the note does not claim the advantage is proven, only that the exception is not a random-sampling case, which is correct.
